name: Erbil International Airport
before:
The busiest airport in the Kurdistan Region of Iraq and third busiest in the country after Baghdad and Al Najaf, serving Erbil.

It has one of the longest runways in the world, a legacy of what the site used to be. The airfield was built by the Ba'athist regime in the early 1970s as an Iraqi military base and stayed military until 1991, when the United Nations imposed a no-fly zone over northern Iraq. After 2003 the Kurdistan Regional Government took over, and a new 550 million dollar airport opened alongside the old one on 5 July 2005.

There are two international airports in the Kurdistan Region, this one and Sulaymaniyah, with a third under construction at Duhok.
after:
Erbil's airport, in the Kurdistan Region of Iraq, handled about 2.1 million passengers in 2024. The runway is one of the longest in the world. It replaced an older airport next door, a military base until 1991.

The FCDO advises against all but essential travel to the Kurdistan Region of Iraq. According to the FCDO, Iran has made strikes and retaliatory attacks in Iraq, including the Kurdistan Region, since 8 July 2026, against US military and civilian infrastructure. The FCDO also notes rocket attacks against the airport and short closures, with operations resuming after a few hours, and says routes in and out of the region, including Erbil and Sulaymaniyah airports, may close at short notice. As the FCDO advises, pre-arrange the transfer and check the flight with the airline before travelling.

claims.claim: replaced an older airport next door
claims.inAfter: It replaced an older airport next door
claims.note: Was 'a new 550 million dollar airport opened alongside the old one on 5 July 2005'. The operator gives a different timeline: the new airport was built from 2005, flights moved across on 1 September 2010 and it was officially opened on 30 March 2011. Wikipedia has 5 July 2005 and USD 550 million. No second source for either set of dates could be saved (the contractor Makyol's site has no Erbil page), so the dates and the cost are dropped and only the undisputed fact is kept.

claims.claim: busiest in the Kurdistan Region; third busiest in Iraq after Baghdad and Al Najaf

claims.why: Wikipedia dates the ranking to 2022 and no current comparison could be saved: the ICAA statistics PDF refuses both fetchers (403) and the statistics office (COSIT) host did not answer. Replaced by the operator's 2024 passenger figure, which Wikipedia's infobox matches.

claims.claim: one of the longest runways, a legacy of the site's past
claims.wasBefore: It has one of the longest runways in the world, a legacy of what the site used to be.
claims.why: The runway claim is kept. The 'legacy' is wrong on both sources: the old airport had a 2,800 m runway, and the 4,800 m runway came with the new airport built by the Kurdistan Regional Government.

claims.claim: built by the Ba'athist regime in the early 1970s
claims.wasBefore: The airfield was built by the Ba'athist regime in the early 1970s as an Iraqi military base and stayed military until 1991
claims.why: The early 1970s date has only Wikipedia. 'Military base until 1991' is kept, with the operator as second source.

claims.claim: the UN no-fly zone ended military use
claims.wasBefore: when the United Nations imposed a no-fly zone over northern Iraq
After 2003 the Kurdistan Regional Government took over
claims.why: Wikipedia says the KRG took over the region, not the airport. The operator says a civil airport was set up on the site in 2003, with the first commercial flight on 15 December 2003; one source, so not added.

claims.claim: new USD 550 million airport opened on 5 July 2005
claims.wasBefore: a new 550 million dollar airport opened alongside the old one on 5 July 2005
claims.why: Contradicted by the operator, which says the new airport was built from 2005, took over flights on 1 September 2010 and was officially opened on 30 March 2011. The cost has only Wikipedia. Softened to 'it replaced an older airport next door'.

claims.claim: two international airports in the Kurdistan Region; a third under construction at Duhok
claims.wasBefore: There are two international airports in the Kurdistan Region, this one and Sulaymaniyah, with a third under construction at Duhok.
claims.why: Time-sensitive and not confirmed: no current source on Duhok's airport could be found. Sulaymaniyah stays in the text through the FCDO's warning, which names both airports.
